\section[el helado]{el helado — something frozen becomes a treat}

\label{lesson:ES-C411-helado}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{el hielo}, ice. Its cold family leads to \textbf{el helado}, ice cream.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Helado} is the participle of \textbf{helar}, to freeze: its first sense is “frozen.” Used as a noun with \textbf{el}, it names ice cream. \textbf{Hielo}, \textbf{helar} and \textbf{helado} all continue the Latin cold-family already met in the ice lesson. The silent \textbf{h} links their modern spelling even though it makes no sound.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: thing or description?}]
With an article, \textbf{el helado} is the food. After a noun, \textbf{helado / helada} can describe something frozen: \textbf{agua helada}. For the mock café message, listen for the noun \textbf{un helado}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el helado}
  \item \emph{un helado de chocolate}
  \item \emph{quiero un helado}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ice cream? (\emph{El helado}.) One chocolate ice cream? (\emph{Un helado de chocolate}.)
